The official getsentry/sentry-api-schema repository publishes the dereferenced OpenAPI 3.0.3 document for the "Sentry Public API" (info title "API Reference", version v0), covering the full /api/0/ surface.

Sentry hosts a public sandbox at sandbox.sentry.io ("Interactive Sandbox... kick our proverbial tires"), an email-gated demo environment pre-populated with sample issue data and isolated from any customer's production data. It is a product-UI demo showroom; nothing documents it as an environment for testing API calls.
The API docs' Versioning section: "The current version of the Sentry's web API is considered v0. Our public endpoints are generally stable, but beta endpoints are subject to change."

Sentry publishes a dedicated API Deprecation Policy on its developer-documentation site (develop.sentry.dev, getsentry-owned), governing how public endpoints are deprecated. The page is engineering-facing documentation of the policy rather than a customer-facing contract page, and the public docs add that the v0 API "is still under development".

An Amazon developer pointed to an Amazon contribution to the Sentry repo and said many developers at Amazon love(d) using Sentry, and one wanted to contribute back in a small way.

Self-hosted Sentry kept growing: each release unleashed more containers and consumed more memory until they couldn't run anything on their 32GB server except Sentry. They evaluated GlitchTip and Bugsink and moved to GlitchTip.
A team running Sentry and GlitchTip side by side found GlitchTip has many more bugs than Sentry, but they are trying to stick with it because it is so much lighter.

GlitchTip replaced their Sentry 9.x ("pre-Clickhouse madness") by just updating the DSN in configs. Its UI is a bit buggy, but it does 99% of what Sentry did with 10% of the effort needed to maintain a modern Sentry setup.
With a small user base (<1000 users), Sentry did not make sense for them. GlitchTip lacks some of Sentry's functionality but covers their needs and has run in production for a year without problems.

A user who loves Sentry said that for a growing business its features are more nice-to-have than critical, and the hosted monthly bill is easy to rack up. They appreciated that self-hosting gives an escape hatch so heavy Sentry integration isn't complete vendor lock-in.

Huge Sentry fans with it deeply integrated in their products: the fully open source code helped a ton with advanced integrations, since they could see exactly what happens instead of relying only on the docs (which are also great). They plan to keep using Sentry despite the BSL change.

They have run self-hosted Sentry at work for a couple of years and it has worked fantastically; once running it is rock-solid. They also use the SaaS. Self-hosted releases take time to appear after SaaS launches.
A happy user on the cloud offering in their early stages likes knowing they can host their own instance if the costs become too much.
Disappointed by the relicensing: they had planned to use Sentry for a side project but now will find an alternative or use an old version, because they refuse to rely on closed-source software.

Long-time customer says Sentry is deeply integrated in their products. Its fully open-source code helped them build advanced integrations because they could read exactly what happens instead of relying on docs, which they also call great. Despite the BSL change they will keep using Sentry and remain customers.
Was planning to implement Sentry for a side project. After the BSL relicensing they will look for an alternative or use an old version, because they refuse to rely on closed-source software.

Has run self-hosted Sentry at work for a couple of years and also uses the SaaS for freelance work. Self-hosted releases appear later than SaaS launches, but once running it is "rock-solid… I never worry about it."

Self-hosts Sentry on Hetzner on a 96-core, 512GB server for about $300/month at roughly 25M transactions per day. They estimate the managed version would cost tens of thousands. Initial headaches: they had to increase Kafka partitions and add replicas to transaction processors, otherwise backpressure filled Redis until it ran out of memory.
Deployed self-hosted Sentry with a Helm chart a while back and "it just works." They had a few incidents over the years that required wiping Kafka queues.
Put off by how much shell script must run to install. A 16GB minimum machine also makes no sense for tracking errors on the 4–8GB VPSes that run their production services.

Uses Sentry with most clients. For effective local debugging they must run their own Sentry in Docker, which is heavy on their machine, especially alongside Grafana and Prometheus. They feel monitoring vendors push lock-in to expensive clouds.

Sentry was straightforward to deploy years ago but is now "self host-able but increasingly prohibitively complex." The only practical way they found to deploy it for clients is Kubernetes plus Helm on bare metal. It runs well if you can throw hardware and engineering time at it.

Has self-hosted Sentry for over 10 years: git clone, edit one or two config files, run ./install.sh. They say 16GB RAM is only needed with the full feature set, such as session replay and end-to-end tracing. They praise the self-hosting team as responsive and helpful on Discord.

At an IoT startup in 2019–2020, using Sentry for distributed tracing pushed the bill to $3–5,000 from tracing alone. They looked into self-hosting and were flabbergasted by the project's complexity, suggesting simpler tracing tools may be the better choice.

Moved away from managed Sentry for GDPR reasons, having used it only for unhandled-exception notifications. They replaced it with a custom Django logging handler that writes to a database table plus daily cron emails. It does far less, but fits their needs.

Uses both hosted and self-hosted Sentry and prefers hosted because there is less to manage. They would only self-host for legal or compliance reasons. Self-hosted truly broke only once in many years, on the upgrade from 9 to date-based versioning, where starting from scratch was easier.

Has self-hosted 2 instances for about 8 years on 20GB RAM and also pays for a hosted one. About 90% of updates went smoothly; the other 10% had problems, all solved via the issue tracker. They are a little afraid of updates but do them every couple of months. They call Sentry "amazing" and a fairly easy self-host.

Recommends Apache SkyWalking as an APM that may not do everything Sentry does. It runs in a far more manageable setup than Sentry's long self-hosted Docker Compose file and can use PostgreSQL, so it doesn't eat RAM.
"too bad the dashboard is slow as molasses"

Recently switched from an old self-hosted version to paid Sentry and says it's mostly been great. But search is clunky: it's very difficult to find anything that doesn't automatically appear on the first page of recent events.
They use Sentry and say it "magically" detects errors in CI that no human would have caught.

Loves Sentry: very responsive support, all open-source code, nice UI, and no nagging for extra services. They call the price very fair, to the point that hosting with Sentry is much cheaper than self-hosting, even though self-hosting is well documented and supported.

Biggest problem: Sentry samples exceptions, so they can't rely on it to view every instance when every exception must be saved. For that reason they wouldn't pick it for their next project, though otherwise it has been a fantastic tool.

Says Sentry has exceptional customer service: prompt, useful responses or bug fixes every time they reached out. They rely on it for crash reporting of native programs in an open-source game engine; without it, resolving user crashes would be "1000x harder." Integration couldn't have been simpler.
